title: Second difference: absolute premotion against relative delight
source_text: LXXV. Deinde juxta Thomistarum mentem, auxilium Physice praedeterminans tale est, ut in quibuscunque circumstantiis voluntas collocetur, semper faciat facere, & operetur effectum suum, omnemque superet resistentiam. Nempe si idem auxilium, quod hunc vel illum hominem ad bene operandum movet & determinat, reliquis omnibus daretur, omnes similiter moveret, adeoque hunc ipsum quibuscunque supponeretur concupiscentiae motibus agitatus. Verum, ex Jansenii sensu, aliter se habet Christi adjutorium efficax. Nam delectatio victrix, in qua adjutorium illud collocat, relativa est. Tunc enim est victrix quando delectatione opposita major est. Quod si contingat alteram ardentiorem esse, in solis inefficacibus desideriis haerebit animus, nec efficaciter unquam volet quod volendum est. Proinde quae in uno victrix est, propter debiliores concupiscentiae motus, in alio superabitur & inefficax erit, propter motus ejusdem concupiscentiae vehementiores. Nec quae in hoc homine ad vincendam praesentem tentationem sufficit, sufficiet alio tempore, si fortior & acrior urgeat tentatio.
pass_a_gloss: LXXV. Then according to the Thomists' mind, the help physically predetermining is such, that in whatever circumstances the will be placed, it always makes it act, and works its effect, and overcomes every resistance. Namely if the same help, which moves and determines this or that man to working well, were given to all the rest, it would move all alike, and so this very man whatever motions of concupiscence he were supposed to be agitated by. But, in Jansenius' sense, the efficacious help of Christ is otherwise. For the victorious delight, in which he places that help, is relative. For it is then victorious when it is greater than the opposite delight. But if it happen that the other is more ardent, the mind will stick in ineffective desires only, nor will it ever efficaciously will what is to be willed. Therefore that which in one is victorious, on account of weaker motions of concupiscence, in another will be overcome and will be inefficacious, on account of more vehement motions of the same concupiscence. Nor will that which in this man suffices to conquer the present temptation, suffice at another time, if a stronger and sharper temptation press.
pass_b_english: Thesis LXXV. Next, in the Thomists' view the physically predetermining aid is such that, whatever the circumstances in which the will is placed, it always makes it act, produces its effect, and overcomes all resistance. If the same aid that moves and determines this or that person to act well were given to everyone else, it would move them all alike, and would move this same person too, whatever impulses of concupiscence he were supposed to be shaken by.

In Jansenius's sense, however, Christ's efficacious aid works otherwise. The victorious delight in which he places that aid is relative: it is victorious only when it is greater than the opposing delight. If the other delight happens to be more ardent, the mind will cling only to ineffective desires and will never effectively will what ought to be willed.

So a delight that wins in one person, because the impulses of concupiscence are weaker, will be overcome and prove inefficacious in another, because the impulses of the same concupiscence are more violent. Nor will what is enough for this person to overcome a present temptation be enough at another time, if a stronger and fiercer temptation presses on him.
